Situation1: They maintain daily communication with their parents, sharing detailed updates and responding promptly to messages.
Expectation2: Raise public awareness about social inequities and marginalized groups
Situation2: They participate in a discussion where recent reports highlight growing barriers affecting these groups.
Story: My phone buzzed for the third time in ten minutes, my mother’s name lighting up the screen. I was sitting in a crowded community center, listening intently as a panelist described the latest obstacles facing immigrants in our city. As an advocate, I was expected to be fully present, to ask questions, and to amplify these stories online. But my mother’s texts kept coming—she wanted to know if I’d eaten, if I was feeling better after last night’s headache, and if I could call her soon. We always talked in the evenings, and she worried if I didn’t reply quickly. I felt the weight of her concern, the unspoken expectation that I would always be available, always attentive. At the same time, I knew my role here was important; people were counting on me to help bring their struggles to light. My phone vibrated again, and I stared at it, torn between the comfort of my family’s daily rituals and the urgency of the voices in this room. My heart pounded as I tried to decide which call to answer first.
